\chapter{Legale o no}

\section[legale]{legale — legal, lawful}

\label{lesson:IT-C390-legale}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the request, then the Italian for the certificate.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: legale}
\textbf{legale} — \textquotedblleft{}legal, lawful\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Se è legale, per me va bene.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{If it is legal, it is fine by me.}
\end{quote}

As a noun, \emph{il legale} is a lawyer: \emph{parlane con il tuo legale}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{legale} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{lēgālis} \textquotedblleft{}of the law\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), from \emph{lēx, lēgis} \textquotedblleft{}law\textquotedblright{}; the everyday \emph{leale} \textquotedblleft{}loyal\textquotedblright{} is the same Latin word, inherited.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{legale}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{legale}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{legale}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for the request, then the Italian for the certificate, then say \emph{legale} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does legale mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Legal, lawful\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[illegale]{illegale — illegal}

\label{lesson:IT-C390-illegale}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the certificate, then the Italian for legal.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: illegale}
\textbf{illegale} — \textquotedblleft{}illegal\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Scaricare film senza pagare è illegale.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Downloading films without paying is illegal.}
\end{quote}

\emph{In- + legale}: before \emph{l} the \emph{n} becomes \emph{l}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{illegale} is a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin \emph{illēgālis} \textquotedblleft{}unlawful\textquotedblright{}, built from \emph{in-} \textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{} and \emph{lēgālis}, on \emph{lēx, lēgis} \textquotedblleft{}law\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{illegale}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{illegale}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{illegale}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for the certificate, then the Italian for legal, then say \emph{illegale} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does illegale mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Illegal\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[lecito]{lecito — permissible, allowed}

\label{lesson:IT-C390-lecito}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for legal, then the Italian for illegal.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: lecito}
\textbf{lecito} — \textquotedblleft{}permissible, allowed\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
È lecito chiedere, ma non insistere.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{It is all right to ask, but do not insist.}
\end{quote}

Stress on the first syllable: \emph{lècito}. Moral as well as legal.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{lecito} comes from Latin \emph{licitus} \textquotedblleft{}allowed, lawful\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), past participle of \emph{licēre} \textquotedblleft{}to be allowed\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{lecito}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{lecito}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for legal, then the Italian for illegal, then say \emph{lecito} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[illecito]{illecito — unlawful, illicit}

\label{lesson:IT-C390-illecito}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for illegal, then the Italian for permissible.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: illecito}
\textbf{illecito} — \textquotedblleft{}unlawful, illicit\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La polizia ha scoperto un traffico illecito di animali.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The police uncovered an illicit trade in animals.}
\end{quote}

As a noun, \emph{un illecito} is an offence: \emph{un illecito amministrativo}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{illecito} comes from Latin \emph{illicitus} \textquotedblleft{}not allowed, unlawful\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), built from \emph{in-} \textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{} and \emph{licitus}, on \emph{licēre} \textquotedblleft{}to be allowed\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{illecito}, once more

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for illegal, then the Italian for permissible, then say \emph{illecito} again
\end{itemize}

\section[abusivo]{abusivo — unauthorised, unlicensed}

\label{lesson:IT-C390-abusivo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for permissible, then the Italian for unlawful.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: abusivo}
\textbf{abusivo} — \textquotedblleft{}unauthorised, unlicensed\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Questa casa è abusiva: non ha i permessi.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{This house is unauthorised: it has no permits.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Un parcheggiatore abusivo} — an unlicensed parking attendant.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{abusivo} comes from Latin \emph{abūsīvus} \textquotedblleft{}misapplied, improper\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{abūsus} \textquotedblleft{}misuse\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{abūtī} \textquotedblleft{}to use up, to misuse\textquotedblright{} and \emph{ūtī} \textquotedblleft{}to use\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
